q: You're following a long lorry. As it approaches a junction on the left, it moves out towards the centre of the road. What should you do?
options: Pass it on the left while there's room
Stay back, as it may be turning left
Overtake it quickly on the right
Sound your horn to warn the driver
explain: Long vehicles may need extra road space to turn, and may move over to the right before turning left. Stay back and be prepared to stop and wait if it needs room or time to turn.

q: You're approaching a roundabout behind a long vehicle that is straddling both lanes. What should you do?
options: Stay back and watch for its signals
Pass it on the left as you enter
Sound your horn so it picks a lane
Overtake it before the roundabout
explain: Because of their length, long vehicles (including those towing trailers) might have to take a different course or straddle lanes, either approaching or on the roundabout. Give them plenty of room and watch out for their signals.

q: At a mini-roundabout, which vehicles may drive over the central markings?
options: Cars that are turning right at them
Any vehicle that's making a U-turn
Large vehicles unable to get round them
Cars that are towing small trailers
explain: All vehicles MUST pass round the central markings at a mini-roundabout, except large vehicles which are physically incapable of doing so. Avoid making U-turns at mini-roundabouts.

q: You're thinking of overtaking a long lorry on a single carriageway road. What should you bear in mind?
options: Its driver must slow down for you
You can cut in sharply once past
Lorries must pull over to let you by
It'll take longer to pass than a car
explain: Overtaking large vehicles is more difficult. It takes longer to pass a large vehicle, so make sure you have enough room to complete the manoeuvre before committing yourself. If in doubt, don't overtake.

q: The car in front of you pulls out to overtake a long lorry. You also want to overtake. What should you do?
options: Follow the car closely past the lorry
Flash the car ahead to make it hurry
Wait until you can see it's safe yourself
Pull out alongside the car
explain: Don't assume you can follow a vehicle ahead which is overtaking a long vehicle. If a problem develops, the driver may abort overtaking and pull back in.

q: You're following a tractor towing a trailer along a country road. Why should you stay well back?
options: Tractors aren't fitted with brake lights
There may be another slow vehicle ahead
Its driver will wave you past soon
Tractors can't use indicators
explain: Getting too close to large vehicles, including agricultural vehicles such as a tractor with a trailer, will obscure your view of the road ahead, and there may be another slow-moving vehicle in front. Dropping back also helps the driver see you in their mirrors.

q: You're driving on a wet dual carriageway behind a lorry that's throwing up a lot of spray. What should you do?
options: Move closer to get out of the spray
Switch to main beam to see through it
Drop back to improve your view
Overtake it on the left
explain: Rain and spray from vehicles can make it difficult to see and be seen. In wet weather keep well back from the vehicle in front; pulling back from a large vehicle improves your ability to see and plan ahead.

q: Many large vehicles are fitted with speed limiting devices. What speed do these restrict them to, even on a motorway?
options: 50 mph
56 mph
60 mph
70 mph
explain: Many large vehicles may be fitted with speed limiters which restrict their speed to 56 mph (90 km/h), even on a motorway. Be patient, as larger vehicles are subject to lower speed limits than cars.

q: It's a very windy day. Which of these vehicles is most likely to be affected by the wind?
options: A small hatchback
A low sports car
A high-sided lorry
A family saloon
explain: High-sided vehicles are most affected by windy weather, but strong gusts can also blow a car, cyclist, motorcyclist or horse rider off course.

q: You're following a goods vehicle of more than 7.5 tonnes on a dual carriageway in England. The national speed limit applies. What's the lorry's speed limit?
options: 40 mph
50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
explain: On a dual carriageway in England and Wales, the national speed limit for goods vehicles of more than 7.5 tonnes maximum laden weight is 60 mph. Be patient, as larger vehicles are subject to lower speed limits than cars.

q: You're driving along a town road. A bus ahead at a bus stop signals to pull out. What should you do?
options: Speed up to pass before it moves
Sound your horn to warn the driver
Flash your lights to keep it waiting
Give way to it if it's safe to do so
explain: Give priority to buses, coaches and trams when you can do so safely, especially when they signal to pull away from stops.

q: You're driving in a city where trams run along the road. Why do you need to take extra care near them?
options: They're quiet and can't steer around you
They must always give way to cars
They only ever travel very slowly
They can swerve to avoid other traffic
explain: Be careful of electric vehicles such as trams and milk floats. Trams move quickly but silently and cannot steer to avoid you.

q: You're driving along a street where trams share the road with other traffic. Which of these should you do?
options: Race trams away from traffic lights
Pass moving trams on the inside
Always give way to trams
Drive along on top of the rails
explain: Always give way to trams. Don't try to race or overtake them, or pass them on the inside, unless they're at tram stops or stopped by tram signals and there's a designated tram lane for you to pass. Avoid driving directly on top of the rails.

q: A tram has stopped at a stop with no platform to pick up passengers. No other route is signed. What should you do?
options: Pass between it and the left kerb
Wait until the tram moves off
Overtake it on the right
Sound your horn and pass slowly
explain: At stops without platforms you MUST NOT drive between a tram and the left-hand kerb when it has stopped to pick up passengers. If there's no alternative route signed, don't overtake the tram – wait until it moves off.

q: A tram is signalling to pull away from a stop. Why should you give it priority if it's safe to do so?
options: Trams aren't fitted with brakes
Tram drivers can't see other traffic
It's an offence to follow a tram
Standing passengers could be injured
explain: Always give priority to trams, especially when they signal to pull away from stops, unless it would be unsafe. They may be carrying large numbers of standing passengers who could be injured if the tram had to make an emergency stop.

q: You see this symbol on a hazard warning plate on a tanker. What does it mean?
options: Corrosive substance
Toxic substance
Radioactive substance
Compressed gas
explain: Certain tank vehicles carrying dangerous goods must display hazard information panels. This diamond symbol shows a corrosive substance. If such a vehicle is involved in an incident, keep well away.

q: You're following a motorcyclist on a wet road where there are tram rails. Why should you take extra care?
options: They may need more space to cross
They must ride between the rails
Motorcycles must stop when trams pass
They're not allowed to cross the rails
explain: Cyclists and motorcyclists should take extra care near tram tracks, especially when the rails are wet, and it's safest to cross them at right angles. Be aware that they may need more space to cross the tracks safely.

q: A bus has stopped at a bus stop on your left, leaving a gap between it and the kerb. What should you do?
options: Pass it on the right when it's safe
Drive through the gap on its left
Sound your horn and pass either side
Flash your lights so it pulls in
explain: Don't overtake between the kerb and a bus or tram when it's at a stop. Look out for people getting off the bus and crossing the road, and give priority to the bus if it signals to pull away.

q: You're in a queue of slow-moving traffic on a town road. What should you be especially aware of?
options: Traffic lights changing more slowly
Motorcyclists passing on either side
Cars being allowed to use bus lanes
Oncoming traffic having to stop
explain: In slow-moving traffic, be aware of cyclists and motorcyclists who may be passing on either side. They're more difficult to see than larger vehicles and their riders are particularly vulnerable.

q: You're approaching a roundabout when an ambulance with flashing blue lights comes up behind you. Why shouldn't you brake harshly?
options: A vehicle behind may not have the same view
Ambulances must give way at roundabouts
The ambulance will always go round you
It's an offence to stop near a roundabout
explain: When an emergency vehicle approaches, don't panic: consider its route and take appropriate action to let it pass. Don't brake harshly on approach to a junction or roundabout, as a following vehicle may not have the same view as you.

q: You're waiting at a red traffic light beside a tramway. The tram next to you moves off while your light is still red. What's the most likely reason?
options: Trams usually have their own signals
Trams can ignore all traffic signals
Your traffic light has stopped working
The tram is answering an emergency call
explain: Tram drivers usually have their own traffic signals and may be permitted to move when you're not. Always give way to trams, and don't try to race them.

q: A powered mobility scooter is being used on the pavement beside the road. What's the maximum speed it may travel at on the pavement?
options: 4 mph
6 mph
8 mph
12 mph
explain: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters MUST NOT travel faster than 4 mph (6 km/h) on pavements or in pedestrian areas. Class 3 vehicles, which can also be used on the road, are restricted to 8 mph (12 km/h).

q: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters can be used on some roads. Where MUST they NOT be used?
options: On motorways
On dual carriageways
On roads without a pavement
On roads with a 40 mph limit
explain: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters MUST NOT be used on motorways. They shouldn't be used on unrestricted dual carriageways where the speed limit exceeds 50 mph, but if they are, they MUST have a flashing amber beacon.

q: You're driving along a main road and see a vehicle ahead showing a flashing amber beacon. What does this usually warn you of?
options: An ambulance on an emergency call
A police car about to stop you
A slow-moving or stationary vehicle
A doctor on an emergency call
explain: Flashing amber beacons warn of a slow-moving or stationary vehicle, such as a traffic officer vehicle, salt spreader, snow plough or recovery vehicle, or an abnormal load. Approach with caution.

q: On an unrestricted dual carriageway, which of these vehicles MUST use a flashing amber beacon?
options: Tractors limited to 25 mph or less
Cars towing caravans or trailers
Vans carrying heavy loads
Lorries over 7.5 tonnes
explain: On unrestricted dual carriageways, motor vehicles first used on or after 1 January 1947 with a maximum speed of 25 mph or less, such as tractors, MUST use a flashing amber beacon.

q: You're driving behind a snowplough on a dual carriageway. When may you overtake it?
options: As soon as there's a gap
Once your intended lane is cleared
Whenever it drops below 20 mph
When it flashes its headlights
explain: Watch out for snowploughs, which may throw out snow on either side. Don't overtake them unless the lane you intend to use has been cleared.

q: Which of these is true about mini motos and motorised 'go ped' scooters?
options: They may be used in cycle lanes
They MUST NOT be used on roads
They may be used on pavements
They're legal on quiet roads
explain: Most mini motos (miniature motorcycles) and motorised scooters (go peds) don't meet the requirements for road vehicles. They MUST NOT be used on roads, pavements, footpaths or bridleways.

q: You're on a motorway behind a works vehicle displaying the sign 'CONVOY VEHICLE NO OVERTAKING'. What MUST you do?
options: Stay behind it and don't pass
Overtake it on the right
Pass it only if it's slowing
Use the hard shoulder to get by
explain: Where a vehicle displays the sign 'CONVOY VEHICLE NO OVERTAKING', you MUST NOT pass it.

q: You're driving along a narrow road. An ambulance using flashing blue lights and its siren comes up behind you. What should you do?
options: Brake hard and stop at once
Mount the pavement to let it pass
Find a safe place to let it pass
Speed up to stay ahead of it
explain: Consider the route of the emergency vehicle and take appropriate action to let it pass, while complying with traffic signs. If necessary pull to the side and stop, but avoid stopping before the brow of a hill, a bend or a narrow section of road, and avoid mounting the kerb.

q: What colour flashing lights are used by traffic officer and incident support vehicles?
options: Blue
Green
Amber
Red
explain: Traffic officer and incident support vehicles use flashing amber lights. Ambulances, fire engines, police, doctors and other emergency vehicles may use flashing blue, red or green lights.

q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A bus lane ahead
A level crossing ahead
Trams crossing ahead
A tram stop ahead
explain: This sign warns of trams crossing ahead. Take extra care: trams move quickly but silently and can't steer to avoid you.

q: Rear marking boards are required on large goods vehicles over 7,500 kg. Where else are the vertical versions of these markings required?
options: On taxis and private hire cars
On powered mobility scooters
On all horse-drawn vehicles
On builders' skips in the road
explain: Large goods vehicle rear markings are fitted to motor vehicles over 7,500 kg and trailers over 3,500 kg. The vertical markings are also required on builders' skips placed in the road and on commercial vehicles or combinations longer than 13 metres.

q: You see this marker on a lorry's load. What does it tell you?
options: Its load overhangs by over 2 metres
The lorry is carrying dangerous goods
The lorry weighs more than 7,500 kg
The lorry is towing a long trailer
explain: Side and end projection markers are required when a load or equipment, such as a crane jib, overhangs the front or rear of a vehicle by more than two metres.

q: You see a plain orange reflective plate like this on the back of a lorry. What does it mean?
options: It's an abnormal load
It's carrying livestock
It's a slow-moving vehicle
It's carrying dangerous goods
explain: Vehicles carrying dangerous goods in packages are marked with plain orange reflective plates. Road tankers and vehicles carrying tank containers of dangerous goods have hazard warning plates.

q: You're driving on a motorway and see this sign on the back of a works vehicle. What does it mean?
options: A works vehicle has closed a lane ahead
The road works end in 800 yards
A contraflow system starts in 800 yards
All lanes are closed for 800 yards
explain: This sign on the back of a works vehicle warns that a lane ahead has been closed by a works vehicle, without cones. Works vehicles may be used to close lanes for repairs on motorways and other high-speed roads, so take special care.
